memories.content: Avoid em dashes in the proposal; split the sentence or use more ordinary punctuation instead.
The user tends to place several independently reviewable claims in one long sentence.
Use first-person active voice for choices and commitments owned by the proposal author so responsibility remains explicit throughout the work plan.
Describe prototype operations that have already been implemented and verified as observed states.
Describe prototype operations not yet implemented or evaluated as plans or expectations.
When a commitment is phrased passively, readers may interpret it as uncertainty, evasiveness, or reluctance to take responsibility.
Use “we” only for decisions and commitments the authors control, not for external facts or actions owned by another party.
The user should use one first-person pronoun consistently for the same authorial role and should not alternate between “I” and “we” unless the responsible party actually changes.
The user tends to hide unsettled commitments behind passive phrases such as “will be considered” or “is expected.”
Split proposal prose into short sentences when a sentence contains more than one independently reviewable claim.
Keep one main claim in each sentence so a reviewer can locate and assess it quickly.
The user tends to repeat em dashes when a sentence already contains several clauses.
Repeated em dashes can shift a reviewer’s attention from the proposal’s argument to suspicion that its prose was generated by AI.
Conduct one review prior to submission focusing solely on the validity of user problems, system interventions, and field evaluation logic.
Cross-check whether research questions align with the core functions of the system.
Cross-check whether field tasks align with representative measures.
Cross-check whether the evidence to be collected aligns with the design and operational decisions to be changed.
Finally verify that the user problem, system intervention, field evaluation, and expected contribution form one coherent logical flow.
HCI reviewers view the validity of design interventions as low if research questions do not connect to system functions.
HCI reviewers view the validity of evaluation plans as low if field tasks fail to generate representative measures.
HCI reviewers view the practical utility of contributions as low if collected evidence cannot change design or operational decisions.
Before submission, conduct a sequential walkthrough with field liaisons of installation failures, operational interruptions, and recovery scenarios.
Verify in one sentence how each proposed contribution could actually alter specific design or operational decisions.
The user must distinguish unconfirmed field partners and equipment from finalized ones so remaining execution risks can be assessed.

analysis.overview: The frames are largely complementary: the reference frame governs proposal prose, authorial responsibility, and claim granularity, while the compared frame governs pre-submission validity and field-readiness checks. Both distinguish settled from unsettled project states, but apply that distinction to different operational subjects.

relations.reason: The shared status distinction is explicitly scoped to prototype operations in one frame and to field partners and equipment in the other, so both operational subjects must remain visible.
relations.summary: Project descriptions should distinguish settled or verified states from unsettled or unconfirmed states.

relations.reason: This is a one-sided prose-granularity principle, including the observed tendency it is intended to correct.
relations.summary: Proposal sentences should contain one independently reviewable main claim and be split when they contain several.

relations.reason: This is a one-sided punctuation policy supported by a usage tendency and its reviewer-facing rationale.
relations.summary: Proposal prose should avoid repeated em dashes, especially in clause-heavy sentences, because they distract reviewers and may suggest AI-generated writing.

relations.reason: This is a one-sided responsibility principle supported by the identified passive-voice tendency and its likely interpretation by readers.
relations.summary: Author-owned choices and commitments should use first-person active voice rather than evasive passive phrasing.

relations.reason: This independently useful one-sided rule excludes external facts and actions owned by other parties from collective authorial voice.
relations.summary: The pronoun “we” should be reserved for decisions and commitments controlled by the authors.

relations.reason: This is an independent one-sided consistency rule about switching between “I” and “we.”
relations.summary: The same authorial role should use one first-person pronoun consistently unless responsibility changes.

relations.reason: This is a one-sided review-stage instruction defining a distinct review pass and its scope.
relations.summary: A dedicated pre-submission review should focus solely on the validity of user problems, system interventions, and field-evaluation logic.

relations.reason: This one-sided alignment check and its reviewer-facing consequence express one underlying validity claim.
relations.summary: Research questions should be cross-checked against core system functions because disconnection weakens perceived intervention validity.

relations.reason: This one-sided alignment check and its reviewer-facing consequence express one underlying evaluation claim.
relations.summary: Field tasks should generate representative measures because misalignment weakens perceived evaluation validity.

relations.reason: These one-sided instructions and their utility rationale express one underlying requirement for decision-relevant contributions.
relations.summary: Collected evidence and each proposed contribution should be tied to specific design or operational decisions they could change.

relations.reason: This is an independently useful one-sided end-to-end coherence check.
relations.summary: The user problem, system intervention, field evaluation, and expected contribution should form one coherent logical flow.

relations.reason: This is an independently useful one-sided operational-readiness walkthrough.
relations.summary: Before submission, field liaisons should sequentially review installation failures, operational interruptions, and recovery scenarios.

reports.compared_only: The compared frame addresses intervention and evaluation validity, contribution utility, logical coherence, and operational walkthroughs with field liaisons.
reports.differences: Both frames require status-sensitive language, scoped respectively to prototype operations and to field partners and equipment.
reports.reference_only: The reference frame addresses atomic sentences, em-dash avoidance, active ownership, and consistent, properly scoped first-person pronouns.
